# H0: μ = 0 vs H1: μ > 0 (one-sided)
# Effect: mean = 0.2, SD = 0.5, so Cohen's d = 0.2/0.5 = 0.4
# Alpha = 0.05, Target power = 0.80

library(pwr)

# Define effect size
mean_diff <- 0.2
sd <- 0.5
cohens_d <- mean_diff / sd

alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80

# For one-sided test, we adjust alpha for two-sided equivalent
# pwr package uses two-sided by default, so we use alpha/2 for one-sided
# Actually, for pwr.t.test with one-sided: alternative="greater" uses the full alpha

# Use pwr.t.test for one-sample t-test
# n = NULL to solve for sample size
# d = effect size (Cohen's d)
# sig.level = alpha
# power = target power
# type = "one.sample"
# alternative = "greater" for one-sided

result <- pwr.t.test(
  n = NULL,
  d = cohens_d,
  sig.level = alpha,
  power = target_power,
  type = "one.sample",
  alternative = "greater"
)

print(result)
cat("\n")
cat("Effect size (Cohen's d):", cohens_d, "\n")
cat("Exact sample size needed:", result$n, "\n")
cat("Minimum integer sample size:", ceiling(result$n), "\n")

# Verify power at the rounded sample size
n_min <- ceiling(result$n)
verified_power <- pwr.t.test(
  n = n_min,
  d = cohens_d,
  sig.level = alpha,
  type = "one.sample",
  alternative = "greater"
)

cat("\nVerification at n =", n_min, ":\n")

    sig.level = alpha,

# Independent verification using non-centrality parameter approach
# For one-sample t-test with one-sided H1: μ > 0

# Given parameters
mean_diff <- 0.2
sd <- 0.5
cohens_d <- mean_diff / sd  # 0.4
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80

# For one-sided test at alpha = 0.05, critical value from standard normal
# (using normal approximation or t-distribution)
# For one-sided t-test: reject H0 if t > t_crit(alpha, df=n-1)

# Non-centrality parameter: lambda = d * sqrt(n)
# Power formula: P(t_{n-1}(lambda) > t_{crit}) = target_power
# where t_{crit} = t_{1-alpha}(n-1)

# We need to solve for n iteratively or use formula

# Analytic approach using t-distribution
# For large n, this approaches normal: Φ(lambda - z_{1-alpha}) ≈ power

# More precisely, for one-sample t-test:
# lambda = d * sqrt(n)
# Power = P(t_{n-1}(lambda) > t_{1-alpha}(n-1))

# Function to compute power given n
compute_power_onesample <- function(n, cohens_d, alpha = 0.05) {
  if (n < 1) return(0)
  df <- n - 1
  lambda <- cohens_d * sqrt(n)
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df = df)  # critical value for one-sided test
  # Power is P(T > t_crit) where T ~ t_{df}(lambda)
  power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df = df, ncp = lambda)
  return(power)
}

# For one-sample t-test with one-sided H1: μ > 0

mean_diff <- 0.2
sd <- 0.5
cohens_d <- mean_diff / sd  # 0.4

# For one-sided test at alpha = 0.05, critical value from standard normal
# (using normal approximation or t-distribution)
# For one-sided t-test: reject H0 if t > t_crit(alpha, df=n-1)

# Non-centrality parameter: lambda = d * sqrt(n)
# Power formula: P(t_{n-1}(lambda) > t_{crit}) = target_power
# where t_{crit} = t_{1-alpha}(n-1)

# We need to solve for n iteratively or use formula

# Analytic approach using t-distribution
# For large n, this approaches normal: Φ(lambda - z_{1-alpha}) ≈ power

# More precisely, for one-sample t-test:
# lambda = d * sqrt(n)
# Power = P(t_{n-1}(lambda) > t_{1-alpha}(n-1))

# Function to compute power given n
compute_power_onesample <- function(n, cohens_d, alpha = 0.05) {
  if (n < 1) return(0)
  df <- n - 1
  lambda <- cohens_d * sqrt(n)
  t_crit <- qt(1 - alpha, df = df)  # critical value for one-sided test
  # Power is P(T > t_crit) where T ~ t_{df}(lambda)
  power <- 1 - pt(t_crit, df = df, ncp = lambda)
  return(power)

# Evidence e1; success=true

# One-sample t-test: minimum sample size for 80% power
# H0: μ = 0 vs H1: μ > 0 (one-sided)
# Effect: mean = 0.2, SD = 0.5, so Cohen's d = 0.2/0.5 = 0.4
# Alpha = 0.05, Target power = 0.80

library(pwr)

# Define effect size
mean_diff <- 0.2
sd <- 0.5
cohens_d <- mean_diff / sd

alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80

# For one-sided test, we adjust alpha for two-sided equivalent
# pwr package uses two-sided by default, so we use alpha/2 for one-sided
# Actually, for pwr.t.test with one-sided: alternative="greater" uses the full alpha

# Use pwr.t.test for one-sample t-test
# n = NULL to solve for sample size
# d = effect size (Cohen's d)
# sig.level = alpha
# power = target power
# type = "one.sample"
# alternative = "greater" for one-sided

result <- pwr.t.test(
  n = NULL,
  d = cohens_d,
  sig.level = alpha,
  power = target_power,
  type = "one.sample",
  alternative = "greater"
)

print(result)
cat("\n")
cat("Effect size (Cohen's d):", cohens_d, "\n")
cat("Exact sample size needed:", result$n, "\n")
cat("Minimum integer sample size:", ceiling(result$n), "\n")

# Verify power at the rounded sample size
n_min <- ceiling(result$n)
verified_power <- pwr.t.test(
  n = n_min,
  d = cohens_d,
  sig.level = alpha,
  type = "one.sample",
  alternative = "greater"
)

cat("\nVerification at n =", n_min, ":\n")
print(verified_power)
cat("Achieved power:", verified_power$power, "\n")

# Also check power at n-1 to confirm it's below 80%
if (n_min > 1) {
  power_at_prev <- pwr.t.test(
    n = n_min - 1,
    d = cohens_d,
    sig.level = alpha,
    type = "one.sample",
    alternative = "greater"
  )
  cat("\nPower at n =", n_min - 1, ":", power_at_prev$power, "\n")
}

# Prepare final result
POWER_AGENT_RESULT=jsonlite::toJSON(
  list(
    results = list(
      list(metric = "sample_size", value = n_min, unit = "participants_total"),
      list(metric = "achieved_power", value = round(verified_power$power, 6), unit = "proportion"),
      list(metric = "power_at_n_minus_1", value = if(n_min > 1) round(power_at_prev$power, 6) else NA, unit = "proportion"),
      list(metric = "cohens_d", value = cohens_d, unit = "standardized")
    )
  ),
  auto_unbox = TRUE,
  digits = 15
)
